vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presents to the ED with a sudden-onset, severe headache that began 2 hours ago while exercising. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She has no prior history of migraines.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity on examination
Photophobia and phonophobia
Onset during physical exertion (Valsalva)
History of uncontrolled hypertension

vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation is brought to the ED by his wife after she noted an abrupt onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking one hour ago. He appears frustrated, unable to form words, and does not follow commands. His right arm and leg are flaccid.

presentationClues.description: Contralateral hemiparesis (right arm and leg > face)
Global aphasia (expressive and receptive)
Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia (gaze preference to the left)
History of atrial fibrillation
Sudden onset of focal neurological deficits

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought to the trauma bay after being struck in the side of the head with a baseball bat. He initially lost consciousness for a minute but then seemed fine, talking and walking around. About an hour later, he became increasingly lethargic and complained of a severe headache before becoming unresponsive.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Direct trauma to the temporal region (pterion)
Injury to the middle meningeal artery
Ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil (uncal herniation)
Contralateral hemiparesis

vignette: A 20-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the ED with a 24-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and confusion. Her roommate notes she has been very sensitive to light and has been vomiting. On exam, she is febrile to 103°F (39.4°C), lethargic, and has a diffuse petechial rash on her trunk and lower extremities.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Positive Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension when hip is flexed)
Positive Brudzinski's sign (passive neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion)
Petechial rash (suggestive of N. meningitidis)
Living in close quarters (dormitory)

vignette: A 34-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of progressive weakness in his legs, making it difficult to walk. He now feels a 'pins and needles' sensation in his feet and hands, and the weakness is starting to affect his arms. He reports having a diarrheal illness about two weeks ago that resolved on its own.

presentationClues.description: Ascending paralysis/weakness
Symmetric lower extremity weakness greater than upper extremity
Areflexia or hyporeflexia (absent knee and ankle jerks)
Recent gastrointestinal or upper respiratory infection (Campylobacter jejuni is classic)
Paresthesias in distal extremities

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider with a 2-month history of double vision and drooping of her right eyelid that worsens in the evening and after reading. She also notes difficulty chewing her food, feeling that her jaw gets 'tired'. She feels her symptoms improve with rest.

presentationClues.description: Fatigable weakness
Ptosis and/or diplopia that worsens with sustained upward gaze
Normal pupillary response and sensation
Symptoms worsen as the day progresses (diurnal variation)
Weakness improves with rest

vignette: A 31-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of blurry vision and pain with movement in her left eye. She also reports a 'tingling' sensation in her legs that occurred a year ago but resolved completely after a few weeks. Examination reveals decreased visual acuity in the left eye and a left afferent pupillary defect.

presentationClues.description: Neurological deficits separated in time and space
Optic neuritis (pain with eye movement, afferent pupillary defect)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock-like sensation down the spine on neck flexion)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Relapsing and remitting sensory or motor symptoms

vignette: A 66-year-old man is brought in by his wife due to concerns about a 'tremor' in his right hand and increasing slowness over the past year. He notes the tremor is worst when he is watching television and goes away when he picks up his coffee cup. He has also developed a 'shuffling' walk and has lost his sense of smell.

presentationClues.description: Pill-rolling tremor at rest
Cogwheel rigidity on passive range of motion
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement, masked facies)
Shuffling, festinating gait
Asymmetric onset of motor symptoms

vignette: An 82-year-old man with a history of falls is brought to the clinic by his daughter for a 3-week history of progressive confusion, lethargy, and gait imbalance. The daughter denies any recent major trauma but recalls he bumped his head on a cabinet about a month ago. He is currently taking aspirin for primary prevention.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient on anticoagulants or antiplatelets
History of minor head trauma weeks prior
Gradual onset of cognitive decline, headache, and focal deficits
Waxing and waning level of consciousness
Bridging vein tear

vignette: A 45-year-old man with a history of chronic low back pain presents to the ED with a 12-hour history of severe, worsening back pain, numbness in his groin and inner thighs, and difficulty urinating. He reports feeling like he can't fully empty his bladder and has had one episode of bowel incontinence. He also notes weakness in both of his feet.

presentationClues.description: Saddle anesthesia
Bilateral lower extremity weakness (e.g., foot drop)
Decreased anal sphincter tone on rectal exam
New-onset urinary retention or overflow incontinence
Bowel incontinence

vignette: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of uncontrolled hypertension presents to the ED with an abrupt onset of severe, sharp chest pain that he describes as a 'tearing' sensation radiating to his upper back. He feels lightheaded and sweaty. On examination, his blood pressure is 180/110 mmHg in the right arm and 130/80 mmHg in the left arm.

presentationClues.description: Tearing or ripping chest pain radiating to the back
Blood pressure differential >20 mmHg between arms
New diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation
History of uncontrolled hypertension
Sudden, maximal intensity pain at onset

vignette: A 55-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with a two-day history of a severely painful, swollen, and red right knee. She is unable to bear any weight on the leg and has a fever of 102.5°F (39.2°C). She reports feeling generally unwell with chills and body aches.

presentationClues.description: Acutely monoarticular arthritis
Significant pain with passive range of motion of the joint
Erythema, swelling, and warmth over a single joint (often the knee)
Systemic symptoms such as fever and chills
Risk factors: pre-existing joint disease, IV drug use, immunosuppression

vignette: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension suddenly collapses while arguing with a family member. He is brought to the ED where he is found to be stuporous, with a GCS of 9. He has a left-sided facial droop, no movement in his left arm or leg, and his eyes are deviated to the right. He vomited once en route.

presentationClues.description: Abrupt onset of focal neurological deficit that worsens over minutes to hours
Symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, decreased consciousness)
Major risk factor: chronic hypertension
Deep coma or stupor early in the course
Gaze deviation towards the side of the lesion

vignette: A 48-year-old man is brought to the hospital with a 3-day history of fever, headache, and bizarre behavior, including personality changes and confusion. In the ED, he has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. His wife notes he had a cold sore on his lip last week.

presentationClues.description: Altered mental status and personality changes are prominent features
Fever and headache
Focal neurological signs (e.g., aphasia, hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsies)
New onset of seizures
Association with HSV-1 (temporal lobe involvement)

vignette: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her son, who is concerned about her memory. He states that for the past two years, she has been progressively more forgetful, frequently misplacing items and repeating questions. Recently, she got lost while driving home from the grocery store, a route she has taken for 40 years.

presentationClues.description: Insidious onset and gradual progression of cognitive decline
Initial prominent deficit in recent memory (anterograde amnesia)
Subsequent development of visuospatial dysfunction (getting lost) and executive dysfunction
Normal motor and sensory exam early in the disease
Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles

vignette: A 35-year-old man with a known seizure disorder is brought to the ED by ambulance. Paramedics state he was found actively convulsing, and he has continued to have generalized tonic-clonic movements for the last 10 minutes without regaining consciousness. His medication compliance has been poor.

presentationClues.description: Seizure lasting > 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them
History of epilepsy with poor medication adherence
Continuous motor activity (convulsive status)
Profoundly altered mental status without motor activity (nonconvulsive status)

vignette: A 26-year-old female presents with a severe, unilateral, throbbing headache that started 30 minutes ago. She reports that prior to the headache, she saw 'flashing zigzag lines' in her right visual field for about 20 minutes. The headache is associated with severe nausea and sensitivity to both light and sound.

presentationClues.description: Scintillating scotoma
Preceding transient neurological symptoms (aura)
Unilateral, pulsating/throbbing quality
Photophobia and phonophobia
Nausea and/or vomiting

vignette: A 72-year-old woman complains of a 6-week history of severe stiffness and aching in her shoulders, neck, and hips. The stiffness is most profound in the morning, lasting for over an hour and making it difficult for her to get out of bed or comb her hair. She also reports fatigue and a low-grade fever.

presentationClues.description: Age > 50 years
Bilateral, symmetric pain and stiffness in proximal joints (shoulders, hips)
Morning stiffness lasting > 45 minutes
Pain on active range of motion of shoulders, normal muscle strength
Associated with Giant Cell Arteritis

vignette: An 80-year-old woman presents with a new-onset, unilateral headache localized to her right temple for the past three weeks. She also reports pain in her jaw when she chews and has had two episodes of transient, curtain-like vision loss in her right eye. On exam, her right temporal artery is tender to palpation and non-pulsatile.

presentationClues.description: New-onset headache in a patient > 50 years old
Jaw claudication
Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness)
Tender, thickened, or pulseless temporal artery
Constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss)

vignette: A 60-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis is brought to the ED with shortness of breath and dizziness. His blood pressure is 85/60 mmHg, heart rate is 120 bpm, and respiratory rate is 24/min. Physical exam reveals markedly distended neck veins, and his heart sounds are faint.

presentationClues.description: Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds
Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop in systolic BP with inspiration)
Tachycardia and tachypnea
History of pericarditis, uremia, malignancy, or recent cardiac surgery
Clear lung fields despite dyspnea

vignette: A 42-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester woke up this morning with a strange sensation in her face. When she looked in the mirror, she noticed the entire right side of her face was drooping. She is unable to close her right eye, raise her right eyebrow, or smile on the right side, and reports altered taste.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of unilateral facial paralysis
Involvement of the upper face (forehead) and lower face
Inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos)
Associated ear pain, hyperacusis, or altered taste
Often preceded by a viral illness (HSV)

vignette: A 38-year-old woman presents with severe, burning pain in her left hand and wrist that began 8 weeks after a minor wrist sprain. The pain is out of proportion to the initial injury. She notes that her hand is now exquisitely sensitive to touch, is often swollen and sweaty compared to the right, and has a bluish discoloration.

presentationClues.description: Pain out of proportion to the initial injury
History of preceding trauma or surgery to the affected limb
Allodynia (pain from a non-painful stimulus) and hyperalgesia
Autonomic dysfunction (changes in skin color, temperature, or sweating)
Edema and/or trophic changes (hair growth, nail changes)

vignette: A 58-year-old man with diabetes and a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a 3-day history of worsening substernal chest pressure. Initially, the pain only occurred with strenuous exertion, but this morning he experienced 15 minutes of chest pressure while watching TV. An ECG shows T-wave inversions in the anterior leads, but his initial troponin level is negative.

presentationClues.description: New-onset angina
Angina that is increasing in frequency, duration, or intensity (crescendo angina)
Angina occurring at rest
Normal or nonspecific ECG changes (ST depression, T-wave inversion)
Negative cardiac enzymes (troponin)

vignette: A 22-year-old man is brought for evaluation after several episodes of 'spacing out.' His girlfriend reports that during these episodes, he will stare blankly for about 90 seconds, making repetitive chewing motions with his mouth. He does not respond to her during the event and is confused for several minutes afterward, with no memory of what happened.

presentationClues.description: Automatisms (lip smacking, chewing, picking at clothes)
Impaired awareness or loss of consciousness
Postictal confusion or amnesia of the event
May be preceded by an aura (e.g., rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu)
Focal onset suggests a specific brain region (often temporal lobe)

vignette: A 65-year-old woman presents to the ED with a sudden onset of vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. She also complains of difficulty swallowing, a hoarse voice, and numbness on the left side of her face and the right side of her body. On examination, she has nystagmus, left-sided ptosis and miosis, and ataxia of her left arm and leg.

presentationClues.description: Crossed sensory findings (ipsilateral face, contralateral body)
Vertigo, nystagmus, nausea, vomiting (vestibular nuclei)
Dysphagia, hoarseness, decreased gag reflex (nucleus ambiguus)
Ipsilateral ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle)
Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis)

vignette: A 52-year-old woman presents to the ED with a sudden-onset severe headache that began 2 hours ago while exercising. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She has no prior history of migraines.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache - sudden, severe onset
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity on examination
Photophobia present
Onset during physical exertion (Valsalva)
No prior history of similar headaches

vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation and hypertension is brought to the ED after his wife noted a sudden onset of confusion and right-sided weakness 1 hour ago. He is unable to speak clearly, and the right side of his face is drooping. His symptoms have been constant since onset.

presentationClues.description: Right hemiparesis (arm > leg)
Expressive aphasia (Broca's area)
Right lower facial droop
History of atrial fibrillation (cardioembolic source)
Sudden onset of focal neurological deficits

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought to the ED after being struck in the side of the head by a baseball. He initially lost consciousness for about a minute but then felt fine and continued to talk for about an hour. He has since become progressively drowsy and is now difficult to arouse.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Trauma to the temporal region (middle meningeal artery)
Ipsilateral fixed and dilated pupil (uncal herniation)
Rapid neurological decline after period of alertness

vignette: A 20-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. He is confused and has developed a non-blanching rash on his trunk and lower extremities. His roommate reports he seemed well yesterday.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Positive Kernig's sign
Positive Brudzinski's sign
Petechial or purpuric rash (suggests N. meningitidis)
Living in close quarters (dormitory)

vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of progressive weakness that started in her feet and is now affecting her thighs and hands. She reports tingling in her fingers and toes but denies any cognitive changes. Two weeks ago, she had a significant bout of gastroenteritis.

presentationClues.description: Ascending paralysis
Areflexia or hyporeflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes)
Symmetric weakness
Recent history of viral or bacterial illness (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni)
Progression of symptoms over days to weeks

vignette: A 28-year-old female presents with a 3-month history of double vision and drooping of her right eyelid that worsens in the evening and after prolonged reading. She also notes her jaw feels tired when chewing tough foods. Her symptoms seem to improve significantly after she rests with her eyes closed.

presentationClues.description: Fluctuating muscle weakness
Fatigability - symptoms worsen with use
Ptosis and/or diplopia
Symptoms improve with rest or application of an ice pack
Difficulty chewing (masseter weakness) or swallowing

vignette: A 31-year-old woman presents with a new onset of numbness and tingling in her left leg that has persisted for 3 days. She recalls an episode of blurry vision and pain in her right eye that resolved on its own about a year ago. She also notes that her symptoms seem to get worse after a hot shower.

presentationClues.description: Neurological symptoms disseminated in time and space
Uhthoff's phenomenon (worsening symptoms with heat)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock-like sensation down the spine on neck flexion)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
History of optic neuritis

vignette: A 67-year-old man presents with a complaint of a tremor in his right hand that has slowly worsened over the past year. His wife has noticed that he walks with a shuffle and his face seems less expressive. The patient notes the tremor is most noticeable when his hand is resting in his lap and improves when he reaches for something.

presentationClues.description: Pill-rolling tremor
Asymmetric resting tremor
Cogwheel rigidity
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement)
Masked facies (hypomimia)

vignette: A 65-year-old man with a long history of uncontrolled hypertension presents with the abrupt onset of a severe, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back, between the scapulae. He feels lightheaded and weak. On examination, he is diaphoretic and in severe distress.

presentationClues.description: Tearing or ripping chest pain radiating to the back
Blood pressure discrepancy >20 mmHg between arms
New-onset aortic regurgitation murmur (diastolic)
Pulse deficits in extremities
History of poorly controlled hypertension or Marfan syndrome

vignette: An 82-year-old man who lives alone is brought in by his son due to several weeks of increasing confusion, drowsiness, and an unsteady gait. The patient has a history of atrial fibrillation for which he takes warfarin and has had several minor falls recently. He complains of a dull, constant headache.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient on anticoagulation
History of falls or minor head trauma
Insidious onset of cognitive decline and gait disturbance
Bridging vein rupture
Fluctuating level of consciousness

vignette: A 76-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of a new, unilateral headache localized to her left temple. She also reports pain in her jaw when she chews and an episode of 'like a curtain coming down' over her left eye that lasted 10 minutes. She feels generally fatigued and has a low-grade fever.

presentationClues.description: Jaw claudication
Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness)
Tender, thickened, or pulseless temporal artery
Age > 50 years
Associated symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica (proximal muscle stiffness)

vignette: A 50-year-old man is brought to the ED by his family for acute-onset confusion, fever, and personality changes over the past 48 hours. He has been acting erratically and experienced a focal seizure this morning. His past medical history is notable for recurrent cold sores.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of fever and focal neurologic signs
Bizarre behavior, personality changes, or aphasia
Temporal lobe involvement
Focal seizures

vignette: A 25-year-old man with a known seizure disorder is brought in by ambulance after being found actively convulsing by his roommate. The seizure has been continuous for approximately 10 minutes without a return to baseline consciousness. His medication bottles at home appear full, suggesting non-adherence.

presentationClues.description: Seizure lasting > 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them
Known seizure disorder with medication non-adherence
Ongoing tonic-clonic activity or postictal state with no lucid interval

vignette: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her daughter, who is concerned about her mother's memory. Over the past few years, she has had increasing difficulty with short-term memory, such as forgetting conversations and misplacing items. Recently, she has started having trouble with managing her finances and has gotten lost while driving in her own neighborhood.

presentationClues.description: Insidious onset and gradual progression of cognitive decline
Initial prominent deficit in short-term memory
Impairment in instrumental activities of daily living (e.g., finances, driving)
Normal motor and sensory exam in early stages

vignette: A 38-year-old man presents to the ED with a 2-day history of sharp, substernal chest pain that worsens when he takes a deep breath or lies flat. He reports that the pain is significantly better when he sits up and leans forward. He had a flu-like illness last week.

presentationClues.description: Pleuritic chest pain
Pain relieved by sitting up and leaning forward
Recent viral URI
Pericardial friction rub heard on auscultation
Diffuse, concave ST-segment elevation on EKG

vignette: A 22-year-old male sustained a closed tibial fracture in a soccer match 6 hours ago and was placed in a cast. He now complains of severe, escalating pain in his lower leg that is not controlled by IV opioids. The pain is especially severe when his toes are passively moved up or down.

presentationClues.description: Pain out of proportion to injury
Pain with passive stretch of affected muscles
Tense, swollen, and firm compartment
Paresthesias (an early sign)
Recent fracture or crush injury, especially with casting

vignette: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis presents with an acutely painful, swollen, and red left knee over the past 24 hours. He is unable to bear any weight on the leg and has a fever of 101.5°F. Examination reveals a large effusion and exquisite tenderness with any range of motion.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of a single, swollen, painful joint
Inability to bear weight
Fever and systemic signs of infection
Risk factors: diabetes, immunosuppression, pre-existing joint disease
Synovial fluid WBC > 50,000/mm³ with neutrophil predominance

vignette: A 52-year-old man with a history of hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide is awakened from sleep by excruciating pain in his right great toe. The joint is visibly swollen, erythematous, and so tender that he cannot tolerate the weight of a bedsheet on it. He reports eating steak and drinking several beers at a party last night.

presentationClues.description: Podagra (inflammation of the first metatarsophalangeal joint)
Sudden, nocturnal onset of severe pain
Triggers: alcohol (beer), red meat, diuretic use
Erythematous, swollen, and exquisitely tender joint
Negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals on arthrocentesis

vignette: A 48-year-old man with a history of a large lumbar disc herniation presents to the ED with a 12-hour history of worsening low back pain, new-onset bilateral leg weakness, and numbness in his perineal region. He reports that he has been unable to urinate for the past 8 hours despite feeling a full bladder. His symptoms began after lifting a heavy piece of furniture.

presentationClues.description: Saddle anesthesia
New onset of urinary retention or incontinence (overflow)
Decreased anal sphincter tone
Bilateral sciatica or leg weakness
Surgical emergency requiring immediate decompression

vignette: A 72-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease presents with the sudden onset of severe dizziness, double vision, and difficulty speaking clearly. He also has trouble walking, veering to one side as if drunk. He denies any one-sided weakness in his arms or legs.

presentationClues.description: The 5 D's: Dizziness (vertigo), Diplopia, Dysphagia, Dysarthria, Dystaxia (ataxia)
Crossed signs (e.g., ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral motor/sensory deficit)
Nystagmus and gait ataxia
Absence of typical MCA/ACA stroke symptoms (hemiparesis, aphasia)

vignette: A 26-year-old female presents with a history of recurrent, severe headaches that are typically preceded by a 20-minute period of seeing flashing, zigzag lines in her right visual field. The headache is a unilateral, pulsating pain behind her left eye, accompanied by intense nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. The headaches last 8-12 hours and are relieved by sleeping in a dark, quiet room.

presentationClues.description: Visual aura (scintillating scotoma)
Unilateral, pulsating quality
Associated photophobia and phonophobia
Aura symptoms are transient and fully reversible
Normal neurological exam between attacks

vignette: A 64-year-old man with a long-standing history of poorly controlled hypertension suddenly develops a severe headache, vomiting, and then rapidly loses consciousness. On arrival to the ED, his GCS is 7 and his blood pressure is 230/130 mmHg. Examination reveals right-sided paralysis and fixed deviation of his eyes to the left.

presentationClues.description: History of chronic, uncontrolled hypertension
Rapid progression of neurological deficits within minutes to hours
Markedly elevated blood pressure
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (vomiting, decreased consciousness)
Eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion

vignette: A 40-year-old male presents with a 2-week history of recurrent, excruciatingly severe pain located behind his right eye, which he describes as a 'hot poker.' The attacks occur 1-2 times daily, often waking him up from sleep, and last for about 60 minutes. During an attack, he becomes very restless, paces the room, and notes his right eye tears and his right nostril becomes congested.

presentationClues.description: Suicide headache
Attacks occur in cyclical 'clusters' with periods of remission
Severe, unilateral, periorbital or temporal pain
Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis, miosis)
Restlessness or agitation during attacks

correctDiagnosis: Lumbar Disc Herniation with L5 Radiculopathy
vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of severe low back pain that radiates down the side of his left leg to the top of his foot after he lifted a heavy box. He complains of associated numbness on the dorsum of the foot and has difficulty walking on his heels. The pain is sharp and electrical in nature.

presentationClues.description: Dermatomal pattern of pain and paresthesia (lateral leg, dorsum of foot)
Positive straight leg raise test
Weakness of great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus)
Difficulty with heel walking
Inciting event of lifting or twisting

vignette: A 60-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of progressive, painless weakness. It started as difficulty with buttons and keys in his right hand, but now involves his entire arm and has started in his left leg. He has also noted frequent muscle twitching all over his body and his speech has become slurred.

presentationClues.description: Combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs
Lower motor neuron signs: fasciculations, muscle atrophy, weakness
Upper motor neuron signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign
Asymmetric limb weakness as the initial symptom
Absence of sensory deficits

vignette: A 52-year-old woman presents to the ED with a sudden-onset severe headache that began 2 hours ago while exercising. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She has no prior history of migraines.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache - sudden, severe onset
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity on examination
Photophobia present
Onset during physical exertion (Valsalva)

vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation, for which he is non-compliant with his medication, presents with the acute onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. His wife notes that he seems to understand her but can only get a few frustrated words out. The symptoms began abruptly 1 hour ago.

presentationClues.description: Contralateral hemiparesis, with arm and face weakness greater than leg weakness
Expressive aphasia (Broca's aphasia)
Homonymous hemianopsia (gaze preference towards the side of the lesion)
History of atrial fibrillation (major risk factor for embolic stroke)
Abrupt onset of focal neurologic deficits

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought to the trauma bay after being struck in the side of the head with a baseball bat. He initially lost consciousness for a minute, then seemed fine and was talking for about an hour. He has since become progressively drowsy and is now difficult to arouse.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Direct trauma to the temporal region (middle meningeal artery injury)
Ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil (CN III compression)
Rapid neurologic deterioration after a period of alertness
Lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma on non-contrast head CT

vignette: An 82-year-old man on apixaban for atrial fibrillation is brought in by his family for waxing and waning confusion and gait instability over the past 2 weeks. The family recalls he had a ground-level fall about a month ago but didn't seek care as he seemed fine. He now complains of a dull, constant headache.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient with history of a fall (even minor)
Anticoagulant use
Gradual onset of neurologic symptoms (e.g., confusion, headache, drowsiness)
Fluctuating level of consciousness
Crescent-shaped (concave) hematoma on non-contrast head CT that crosses suture lines

vignette: A 19-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the ED with a 24-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. He is confused and lethargic. On examination, he has a diffuse petechial rash on his trunk and lower extremities.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Positive Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension when hip is flexed)
Positive Brudzinski's sign (passive neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion)
Petechial or purpuric rash (suggests N. meningitidis)
Living in close quarters (dormitory, military barracks)

vignette: A 35-year-old female presents with a 3-day history of progressive weakness that started in her feet and is now affecting her knees and hands, making it difficult to walk or grip objects. She reports tingling in her fingers and toes. Two weeks ago, she had a self-limited episode of watery diarrhea that resolved on its own.

presentationClues.description: Ascending paralysis/weakness
Areflexia or hyporeflexia (loss of deep tendon reflexes)
Symmetric weakness
Recent gastrointestinal (Campylobacter jejuni) or respiratory infection
Albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (high protein, normal WBC count)

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with complaints of double vision and drooping of her right eyelid that worsens significantly in the evening and after reading. She also notes that her jaw gets tired when she chews tough food. Symptoms seem to improve after a short nap.

presentationClues.description: Fatigability (muscle weakness that worsens with repetitive use)
Ptosis and/or diplopia, often asymmetric
Bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia, difficulty chewing)
Symptoms improve with rest
Improvement of ptosis with ice pack test

vignette: A 32-year-old woman from the Pacific Northwest presents with a new onset of numbness and tingling in her left leg and a feeling of a tight band around her waist. She recalls an episode of painful, blurry vision in her right eye last year that resolved on its own. She also notes that her symptoms seem to worsen after a hot shower.

presentationClues.description: Neurologic symptoms disseminated in time and space
History of optic neuritis (pain with eye movement, vision loss)
Uhthoff's phenomenon (worsening of symptoms with heat)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock-like sensation down the spine on neck flexion)
Oligoclonal bands in CSF

vignette: A 67-year-old man is brought in by his wife due to increasing difficulty with his daily activities. She notes he has become very slow, has trouble initiating movement, and has a noticeable tremor in his right hand, especially when he is watching TV. His face seems less expressive than it used to, and his handwriting has become nearly illegible.

presentationClues.description: Resting, pill-rolling tremor
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement)
Cogwheel rigidity on passive range of motion
Shuffling gait and postural instability
Masked facies (hypomimia) and micrographia

vignette: A 45-year-old man is brought to the ED for acute onset of fever, headache, and bizarre behavior over the last 48 hours. His family reports he has been paranoid, having olfactory hallucinations, and had a focal seizure this morning. His past medical history is unremarkable.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of fever, headache, and altered mental status
Bizarre behavior, personality changes, or psychosis
New onset focal seizure
Temporal lobe involvement on MRI or EEG
CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and increased RBCs (in absence of traumatic tap)

vignette: A 62-year-old man with a long history of poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the ED after he suddenly grabbed his head, complaining of a severe headache, and then became unresponsive. On exam, his blood pressure is 220/125 mmHg, he has dense right-sided paralysis, and his eyes are deviated to the left. He withdraws only to painful stimuli.

presentationClues.description: History of chronic, uncontrolled hypertension
Abrupt onset of focal deficit that worsens over minutes to hours
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., vomiting, stupor, coma)
Gaze deviation toward the side of the bleed (away from the hemiparesis)
Hemorrhage typically located in basal ganglia, pons, thalamus, or cerebellum

vignette: A 38-year-old woman with a known history of a seizure disorder is brought in by EMS for a seizure that has been ongoing for at least 10 minutes. According to her roommate, she had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure and has not regained consciousness. On arrival, she is still having convulsive movements.

presentationClues.description: Continuous seizure activity for > 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without a return to baseline consciousness between them
Known history of epilepsy or a precipitating factor (e.g., medication non-compliance, metabolic disturbance)
Ongoing tonic-clonic or other seizure activity upon examination

vignette: A 78-year-old woman is brought in by her son who is concerned about her memory. He notes she has been asking the same questions repeatedly and has trouble managing her finances, a task she previously handled with ease. This has been getting progressively worse over the last 3 years.

presentationClues.description: Insidious onset and gradual progression
Initial prominent deficit in recent memory (anterograde amnesia)
Impairment in executive function (e.g., planning, financial management)
Visuospatial deficits (e.g., getting lost in familiar places)
Normal motor and sensory exam early in the disease course

vignette: A 25-year-old female presents with a history of recurrent, severe headaches. She states that before the headache begins, she sees flashing, zig-zag lines in her right visual field for about 20 minutes. This is followed by a unilateral, pulsating headache associated with nausea and a desire to be in a dark, quiet room.

presentationClues.description: Visual aura (e.g., scintillating scotoma, photopsia) preceding headache
Unilateral, pulsating or throbbing headache
Associated photophobia and phonophobia
Nausea and/or vomiting during the headache
Normal neurological examination between attacks

vignette: A 58-year-old man presents with a 9-month history of progressive weakness. It started as clumsiness in his right hand, making it hard to button his shirt, but now his entire right arm is weak and he has developed slurred speech. He notes visible twitching in his arm and shoulder muscles.

presentationClues.description: Combination of upper motor neuron (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) signs
LMN signs: muscle atrophy, fasciculations, flaccid weakness
UMN signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign
Bulbar involvement (dysarthria, dysphagia)
Preservation of sensation, cognition, and extraocular movements

vignette: A 66-year-old man with a history of untreated hypertension presents with the sudden onset of a severe, 'tearing' chest pain that radiates to his back between the shoulder blades. While being evaluated, he develops acute left leg weakness and paresthesias. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg in the right arm and 145/80 mmHg in the left.

presentationClues.description: Sudden onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest or back pain
Blood pressure differential > 20 mmHg between arms
Pulse deficits in extremities or carotid arteries
Focal neurologic deficits (stroke, paraplegia, syncope)
Widened mediastinum on chest X-ray

vignette: A 72-year-old man with multiple vascular risk factors describes several brief episodes over the past month where he suddenly feels dizzy, sees double, has slurred speech, and feels like he might fall. Each episode lasts about 15 minutes and resolves completely. He denies headache or weakness on one side of his body.

presentationClues.description: Posterior circulation symptoms
The 4 D's: Dizziness (vertigo), Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysphagia (and Ataxia)
Transient, fully resolving neurologic deficits
Multiple vascular risk factors (HTN, HLD, DM, smoking)

vignette: A 45-year-old male with a history of a large L4-L5 disc herniation presents to the ED with acute worsening of his low back pain, now with bilateral leg weakness. He reports numbness in his groin and inner thighs and states that he has not been able to urinate for the last 12 hours despite feeling the urge to go. His symptoms started this morning.

presentationClues.description: Saddle anesthesia (numbness in the perineum, buttocks, and inner thighs)
New onset urinary retention or incontinence
Bowel incontinence or decreased anal sphincter tone
Bilateral sciatica or leg weakness
Decreased deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities

vignette: A 71-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of debilitating pain and stiffness in her shoulders and hips. The stiffness is worst upon waking and lasts for several hours, making it difficult for her to get out of bed or raise her arms to comb her hair. She also reports fatigue and a 10-pound weight loss.

presentationClues.description: Patient age > 50
Bilateral proximal joint (shoulder and hip girdle) aching and stiffness
Morning stiffness lasting > 45 minutes
Markedly elevated ESR (>40 mm/hr) and/or CRP
Rapid, dramatic response to low-dose corticosteroids

vignette: A 76-year-old woman presents with a new, throbbing headache localized to her right temple for the past 2 weeks. She also reports pain in her jaw when she eats a steak and had a brief episode yesterday where it felt like 'a curtain came down' over her right eye. On exam, her right temporal artery is tender to palpation and feels firm.

presentationClues.description: New-onset headache in a patient age > 50
Jaw claudication
Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss)
Tender, thickened, or pulseless temporal artery
Associated symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica

vignette: A 58-year-old man with a known history of chronic alcohol use disorder is brought to the ED from a shelter for being confused and unsteady on his feet. On exam, he is disoriented to time and place, has horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, and walks with a slow, wide-based gait. He cannot perform tandem walking.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: encephalopathy (confusion), oculomotor dysfunction, gait ataxia
History of chronic alcoholism or malnutrition
Nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, or conjugate gaze palsy
Wide-based, ataxic gait
Precipitated by administration of glucose before thiamine

vignette: A 62-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of recurrent, severe facial pain. She describes it as an 'electric shock' on the right side of her cheek that lasts for a few seconds and occurs in volleys. The pain is triggered by brushing her teeth, eating, or even a light breeze on her face.

presentationClues.description: Paroxysmal, lancinating, or electric shock-like pain
Unilateral pain in the distribution of cranial nerve V (V2/V3 most common)
Presence of specific triggers (e.g., touch, chewing, talking)
Pain episodes are brief but can occur in rapid succession
Completely normal neurologic examination between attacks

vignette: A 34-year-old man presents with a 1-day history of left-sided facial paralysis that he first noticed this morning when he tried to drink his coffee. He reports he cannot raise his left eyebrow, close his left eye tightly, or smile on the left side. He also notes that sounds seem louder in his left ear and food tastes bland.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of unilateral upper and lower facial paralysis
Inability to wrinkle the forehead on the affected side
Incomplete eye closure (lagophthalmos)
Flattening of the nasolabial fold and drooping of the corner of the mouth
Associated hyperacusis or decreased taste on anterior tongue

vignette: A 40-year-old construction worker presents with acute low back pain that started after he lifted a heavy bag of cement. The pain is severe and radiates from his right buttock down the back of his thigh and calf to the sole of his foot. He states coughing or sneezing makes the leg pain significantly worse.

presentationClues.description: Radicular pain in a dermatomal pattern (S1 in this case)
Positive straight leg raise test reproduces radicular pain
Weakness of plantar flexion and diminished Achilles reflex (S1)
Inciting event of lifting or twisting
Pain worsened by Valsalva maneuvers (coughing, sneezing, straining)

vignette: A 42-year-old woman who sustained a right wrist fracture 2 months ago, which was treated with a cast, presents with persistent pain that she rates as 10/10. She describes a severe burning sensation that is present even at rest and is excruciating with light touch. Her right hand is swollen, purplish, and colder than her left hand.

presentationClues.description: Pain out of proportion to the initial injury
Preceded by an injury or surgery to the affected limb
Sensory abnormalities: allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli) and hyperalgesia
Autonomic dysfunction: changes in skin color, temperature, swelling, or sweating
Motor/trophic changes: decreased range of motion, weakness, changes in hair/nail growth

vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presents to the ED with a sudden-onset severe headache that began 2 hours ago while exercising. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She has no prior history of migraines.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity on examination
Onset during physical exertion
History of hypertension or polycystic kidney disease

vignette: A 71-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation is brought to the emergency department after his wife noted acute onset of confusion and right-sided weakness 1 hour ago. He is unable to speak coherently, only producing nonsensical words, and seems frustrated. He is also unable to follow commands involving his right arm or leg.

presentationClues.description: Contralateral hemiparesis (right side)
Expressive (Broca's) or Receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia
Homonymous hemianopsia (gaze preference to side of lesion)
History of atrial fibrillation
Abrupt onset of focal neurologic deficit

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought to the ER after being struck in the side of the head by a baseball. He briefly lost consciousness but then felt fine and was talking normally for about an hour. He has since developed a severe headache, vomiting, and is becoming increasingly drowsy.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Direct trauma to the temporal or parietal bone
Ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil ('blown pupil')
Contralateral hemiparesis
Mechanism involves injury to middle meningeal artery

vignette: An 82-year-old man on aspirin for primary prevention is brought in by his family due to a 3-week history of progressive confusion, gait instability, and intermittent headaches. His daughter recalls he had a minor fall where he bumped his head about a month ago but did not seek medical attention. He has become increasingly forgetful and has had several near-falls at home.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient or patient with history of alcoholism (cerebral atrophy)
Minor head trauma weeks to months prior
Tearing of bridging veins
Insidious onset of cognitive decline and focal neurologic deficits
Use of anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents

vignette: A 66-year-old woman with a long history of poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the ED after a sudden collapse. Her husband reports she complained of a severe headache and then became unresponsive. In the ED, her blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg, and she withdraws her left side to painful stimuli but has no movement on the right.

presentationClues.description: Long-standing, poorly controlled hypertension
Abrupt onset of neurologic deficit that worsens over minutes to hours
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., vomiting, bradycardia, decreased consciousness)
No history of trauma
Hypertensive emergency causing neurologic symptoms

vignette: A 19-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and confusion. On examination, he is lethargic, has a temperature of 103.5°F (39.7°C), and is resistant to passive neck flexion. A faint, non-blanching petechial rash is noted on his trunk and lower extremities.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Positive Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension when hip is flexed)
Positive Brudzinski's sign (passive neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion)
Petechial or purpuric rash (suggests N. meningitidis)
Living in close quarters (dormitory, military barracks)

vignette: A 45-year-old man is brought to the hospital by his family due to a 3-day history of escalating fever, headache, and bizarre behavior. He has been having auditory hallucinations, is uncharacteristically aggressive, and seems profoundly confused. He had one witnessed focal seizure this morning prior to arrival.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of fever and focal neurologic signs
Personality changes, bizarre behavior, or psychosis
Temporal lobe involvement
Aphasia or focal seizures
No nuchal rigidity or signs of pure meningitis

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of progressive weakness that started in her feet and has now moved up to her thighs, making it difficult to walk. She also reports tingling in her fingertips and toes. She recalls having a diarrheal illness about two weeks ago that resolved on its own.

presentationClues.description: Ascending symmetric paralysis/weakness
Recent history of URI or gastroenteritis (especially Campylobacter jejuni)
Areflexia or hyporeflexia (loss of deep tendon reflexes)
Paresthesias often precede weakness
Albumino-cytologic dissociation in CSF (high protein, normal WBC)

vignette: A 31-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of blurry vision and pain with eye movement in her right eye. She also mentions an episode of numbness and tingling in her left leg that lasted for a few weeks last year but resolved completely. On exam, she has a right afferent pupillary defect and reduced color vision in the affected eye.

presentationClues.description: Neurologic symptoms disseminated in time and space
Optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss, afferent pupillary defect)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock sensation down spine with neck flexion)
Relapsing-remitting pattern of neurologic deficits

vignette: A 25-year-old woman presents with complaints of double vision and drooping of her eyelids that is minimal in the morning but worsens significantly by the end of the day. She also notes difficulty chewing her food during dinner and her speech becomes slurred after prolonged conversation. Symptoms improve after a period of rest.

presentationClues.description: Fatigable muscle weakness
Symptoms worsen with repetitive use and improve with rest
Ptosis and/or diplopia are common initial symptoms
Positive ice pack test (improvement of ptosis with cold)
Associated with thymoma or thymic hyperplasia

vignette: A 68-year-old man is brought to clinic by his wife, who is concerned about a tremor in his right hand that occurs when he is watching television but disappears when he reaches for his coffee cup. She has also noticed he walks with small, shuffling steps and has a very soft voice. On exam, he has a stooped posture and demonstrates cogwheel rigidity in his upper extremities.

presentationClues.description: Pill-rolling resting tremor
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement)
Cogwheel rigidity
Shuffling or festinating gait (postural instability)
Masked facies (reduced facial expression)

vignette: A 55-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive weakness and clumsiness in his right hand, making it difficult to button his shirt or use a key. He also reports frequent muscle twitching in his arms and cramping in his calves. On examination, there is marked atrophy and fasciculations in his right arm, with hyperreflexia in his lower extremities and a positive Babinski sign.

presentationClues.description: Combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs
Lower motor neuron signs: fasciculations, atrophy, weakness
Upper motor neuron signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign
Asymmetric limb weakness is a common initial presentation
Sensation, bowel/bladder function, and cognition are typically spared

vignette: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the ED by her roommate, who found her confused and lethargic on the floor. The roommate heard a loud cry from the patient's room, followed by several minutes of rhythmic shaking. On exam, the patient is slowly regaining awareness, complains of a headache and sore muscles, and has a laceration on the side of her tongue.

presentationClues.description: Witnessed loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic (stiffening and jerking) movements
Postictal state (confusion, lethargy, focal weakness)
Tongue biting (lateral aspect)
Urinary or fecal incontinence during the event
Patient has no memory of the event

vignette: A 35-year-old man with a known seizure disorder is brought to the emergency department by paramedics. He was witnessed to have a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that has continued for approximately 10 minutes without any return to consciousness. In the ambulance, he was given one dose of IM midazolam with no effect.

presentationClues.description: Seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them
History of epilepsy, often with medication non-compliance
Can be caused by acute CNS insult, metabolic disturbance, or drug withdrawal
Continuous convulsive activity on arrival

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent, severe headaches that she describes as a unilateral, throbbing pain, usually behind her left eye. She reports that for about 20 minutes before the headache begins, she sees flashing, zig-zagging lights in her visual field. The headaches are associated with severe nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, lasting 6-8 hours if untreated.

presentationClues.description: Scintillating scotoma or visual aura
Unilateral, pulsating/throbbing quality
Associated photophobia and phonophobia
Nausea and/or vomiting
Aura is a transient, reversible focal neurologic symptom that precedes the headache

vignette: A 42-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of recurrent, excruciating headaches. He states they occur 1-2 times per day, often waking him from sleep, and consist of a sharp, stabbing pain behind his right eye that lasts for about 45 minutes. During the attacks, his right eye waters profusely, his right nostril becomes congested, and he feels intensely agitated, often pacing the room.

presentationClues.description: Suicide headache
Severe, unilateral, periorbital, or temporal pain
Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, ptosis)
Attacks occur in cyclical 'clusters' with periods of remission
Sense of restlessness or agitation during attacks

vignette: A 76-year-old woman is brought to clinic by her son who is concerned about her memory. He reports that over the last two years, she has had progressive difficulty with short-term memory, such as forgetting conversations and misplacing items. More recently, she has gotten lost while driving in her own neighborhood and is struggling to manage her finances, a task she previously handled with ease.

presentationClues.description: Insidious onset and gradual progression of cognitive decline
Amnesia (memory impairment) is the most prominent early feature
Impairment in instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) like managing finances or medications
Visuospatial deficits (e.g., getting lost in familiar places)
Absence of other neurologic, psychiatric, or systemic diseases that could account for the decline

vignette: A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care with the acute onset of left-sided facial drooping that he first noticed this morning when trying to drink his coffee. He is unable to close his left eye completely, and his smile is asymmetric. He denies any limb weakness, sensory changes, or vision problems and notes that food tastes 'funny.'

presentationClues.description: Unilateral facial paralysis involving both upper and lower face
Inability to wrinkle the forehead on the affected side
Acute onset over hours to 1-2 days
Posterior auricular pain may precede paralysis
Hyperacusis (increased sensitivity to sound) or altered taste

vignette: A 58-year-old homeless man with a known history of chronic heavy alcohol use is brought to the ED by police for confusion. On examination, he is disoriented, has a wide-based, unsteady gait, and demonstrates horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze. He cannot recall how he got to the hospital or what he ate today.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, gait ataxia
Nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, or conjugate gaze palsy
Ataxic gait (wide-based and unsteady)
Altered mental status (confusion, disorientation, apathy)
History of chronic alcoholism or malnutrition (thiamine deficiency)

vignette: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of severe, progressive low back pain, bilateral leg pain, and numbness in his groin area. He reports feeling like he needs to urinate but is unable to, and he has had one episode of bowel incontinence. On exam, he has decreased sensation in a 'saddle' distribution and absent ankle reflexes bilaterally.

presentationClues.description: Saddle anesthesia
New onset urinary retention or incontinence
Bowel incontinence
Bilateral sciatica or leg weakness
Decreased anal sphincter tone on digital rectal exam

vignette: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis presents with a 2-day history of severe right knee pain, swelling, and an inability to bear weight. She denies any recent trauma but reports feeling feverish and unwell. On examination, her right knee is erythematous, exquisitely tender to palpation, and held in a flexed position; passive range of motion elicits extreme pain.

presentationClues.description: Single, hot, swollen, painful joint
Inability to bear weight on the affected limb
Severe pain with passive range of motion
Risk factors: diabetes, immunocompromised state, pre-existing joint disease (RA), IV drug use
Systemic symptoms such as fever and chills

vignette: A 72-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of severe aching and stiffness in her shoulders, neck, and hips. The stiffness is worst in the morning, lasting for over an hour and making it difficult for her to get out of bed or comb her hair. She also reports fatigue and a low-grade fever, and her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is found to be 95 mm/hr.

presentationClues.description: Age > 50 years
Bilateral, symmetric aching and morning stiffness in proximal joints (shoulders, hips, neck)
Markedly elevated ESR and/or CRP
Rapid, dramatic response to low-dose corticosteroids
Strong association with Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis

vignette: A 48-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of progressive difficulty climbing stairs, getting up from a chair, and lifting her arms to wash her hair. Over the same period, she has developed a purplish rash on her eyelids and scaly, red papules over her knuckles. She also reports difficulty swallowing solid foods.

presentationClues.description: Progressive, symmetric proximal muscle weakness
Heliotrope rash (violaceous eruption on upper eyelids)
Gottron's papules (erythematous papules over bony prominences, especially knuckles)
Shawl sign (rash over shoulders, neck, upper chest) or V-sign (rash on anterior neck)
Increased risk of underlying malignancy

vignette: A 65-year-old man with a history of uncontrolled hypertension presents to the ER with the abrupt onset of a severe, tearing chest pain that radiates to his upper back. He feels lightheaded and weak. On examination, his blood pressure is 180/100 mmHg in the right arm and 110/60 mmHg in the left arm, and he has a new, soft diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation.

presentationClues.description: Sudden onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest or back pain
History of chronic hypertension (most common risk factor)
Blood pressure differential >20 mmHg between arms
Pulse deficits in extremities
New aortic regurgitation murmur

vignette: A 32-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents with a 2-week history of daily fevers, chills, and night sweats. Today, he developed acute confusion and weakness of his right arm. On examination, he has a temperature of 102.8°F (39.3°C), a new holosystolic murmur at the apex, and several tender nodules on his fingertips.

presentationClues.description: Risk factor: IV drug use, prosthetic valve, or recent dental procedure
Fever and a new or changing heart murmur
Peripheral stigmata: Osler nodes (painful nodules), Janeway lesions (painless macules), splinter hemorrhages
Systemic embolization causing stroke, renal infarct, or splenic infarct
Roth spots on funduscopic exam

vignette: A 52-year-old woman presents to the ED with a sudden-onset severe headache that began 2 hours ago while exercising. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She has no prior history of migraines.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache - sudden, severe onset
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity on examination
Photophobia present
Onset during physical exertion (Valsalva)

vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation is brought to the ED after his wife noted an acute onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking 1 hour ago. He appears frustrated as he is unable to formulate words clearly. His right arm and face show more pronounced weakness than his right leg.

presentationClues.description: History of atrial fibrillation (embolic source)
Contralateral hemiparesis (arm and face > leg)
Aphasia (expressive/Broca's if dominant hemisphere)
Homonymous hemianopsia
Uncontrolled hypertension

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought in after being struck in the head by a baseball bat during a game. He briefly lost consciousness, but then felt fine and continued playing for about 30 minutes before developing a severe headache, vomiting, and confusion. On arrival, he is drowsy and difficult to arouse.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Trauma to the temporal bone (pterion)
Ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil (CN III compression)
Contralateral hemiparesis
Lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma on non-contrast CT

vignette: An 82-year-old man with a history of falls is brought in by his family for a gradual 3-week decline in cognitive function, increased drowsiness, and mild headaches. His family reports he seems more forgetful and unsteady on his feet. He takes aspirin daily for cardiovascular prevention.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient with brain atrophy
History of minor head trauma or falls
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
Insidious onset of cognitive changes
Crescent-shaped (concave) hematoma on non-contrast CT

vignette: A 20-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the ED with a 24-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. He is confused and has vomited twice. On exam, he has a petechial rash on his trunk and extremities.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Positive Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension)
Positive Brudzinski's sign (neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion)
Living in close quarters (dormitory)
Petechial rash (suggests N. meningitidis)

vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of progressive weakness that started in her feet and has now moved up to her thighs and hands. She reports tingling in her fingers and toes. Two weeks ago, she had a bout of gastroenteritis that resolved on its own.

presentationClues.description: Ascending symmetric weakness/paralysis
Recent history of URI or GI infection (Campylobacter jejuni)
Areflexia or hyporeflexia (loss of deep tendon reflexes)
Albumino-cytologic dissociation in CSF (high protein, normal WBC)
Minimal sensory deficits despite paresthesias

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with several months of intermittent double vision and drooping of her eyelids, which are noticeably worse in the evening. She also notes difficulty chewing her food and her speech becomes slurred after talking for a few minutes. Symptoms seem to improve after a short rest.

presentationClues.description: Fluctuating, fatigable muscle weakness
Worse at the end of the day or with repeated use
Ptosis and/or diplopia (ocular muscle weakness)
Weakness improves with ice pack test
Bulbar symptoms (difficulty chewing, swallowing, speaking)

vignette: A 31-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of blurry vision and pain with eye movement in her left eye. She also reports a strange 'electric shock' sensation that radiates down her spine when she flexes her neck. She recalls an episode of numbness in her right leg six months ago that resolved spontaneously.

presentationClues.description: Symptoms disseminated in time and space
Optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock down spine with neck flexion)
Young female patient (classic demographic)
Oligoclonal bands in CSF

vignette: A 66-year-old man is brought to clinic by his wife due to concerns about his slowness of movement and a tremor in his right hand. He notes his handwriting has become very small and he has difficulty initiating movements, like getting out of a chair. His wife also mentions that he has a 'blank stare' and shuffles his feet when he walks.

presentationClues.description: Resting, pill-rolling tremor
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement)
Cogwheel rigidity
Shuffling, festinating gait with postural instability
Masked facies (hypomimia)

vignette: A 45-year-old man with a history of chronic low back pain presents to the ED with a new onset of severe, radiating leg pain, numbness in his groin and buttocks, and difficulty urinating over the past 12 hours. He states he feels like he needs to urinate but cannot, and he has noticed some dribbling. On exam, he has decreased sensation in the perineal region.

presentationClues.description: Saddle anesthesia
Bowel or bladder dysfunction (urinary retention or incontinence)
Decreased anal sphincter tone
Bilateral sciatica or leg weakness
History of large central disc herniation

vignette: A 72-year-old woman complains of bilateral leg pain, numbness, and weakness that occurs after walking for about 10 minutes. She notes the pain is relieved almost immediately by sitting down or leaning forward over her shopping cart. She denies any pain while sitting or riding a stationary bicycle.

presentationClues.description: Neurogenic claudication
Pain worsened by walking or standing (lumbar extension)
Pain relieved by sitting or leaning forward (lumbar flexion)
Shopping cart sign
Older patient with degenerative spine changes

vignette: A 75-year-old woman presents with a new, throbbing headache localized to her left temple for the past two weeks. She also reports pain in her jaw when she chews and some transient episodes of vision loss in her left eye, which she describes as a 'curtain coming down.' On examination, her left temporal artery is tender to palpation and non-pulsatile.

presentationClues.description: Age > 50
Jaw claudication
New-onset localized headache
Tender, thickened temporal artery
Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss)
Markedly elevated ESR and CRP

vignette: A 68-year-old woman complains of a 1-month history of severe aching and stiffness in her shoulders, neck, and hips. The stiffness is most profound in the morning, lasting for over an hour and making it difficult for her to get out of bed or comb her hair. She also reports general fatigue and a low-grade fever.

presentationClues.description: Age > 50
Bilateral proximal joint aching and stiffness (shoulders, hips)
Morning stiffness lasting > 45 minutes
Strong association with Giant Cell Arteritis
Rapid response to low-dose corticosteroids

vignette: A 65-year-old man with a long-standing history of uncontrolled hypertension presents to the emergency department with an abrupt onset of severe, sharp chest pain that he describes as 'ripping' and radiating to his upper back between the shoulder blades. On examination, his blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg in the right arm and 150/90 mmHg in the left arm. A faint, early diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal border.

presentationClues.description: Severe, tearing or ripping chest pain
Radiation of pain to the interscapular area
Blood pressure differential > 20 mmHg between arms
New aortic regurgitation murmur
History of uncontrolled hypertension or Marfan syndrome

vignette: A 35-year-old man presents with sharp, retrosternal chest pain that started two days ago. The pain is worse when he lies down or takes a deep breath, and he finds some relief by sitting up and leaning forward. He reports having a 'bad cold' with a fever and cough about a week prior.

presentationClues.description: Pleuritic chest pain (worse with inspiration)
Positional pain: worse supine, improved by leaning forward
Pericardial friction rub
Diffuse ST-segment elevation on EKG
Recent viral illness (URI)

vignette: A 42-year-old man with a history of IV drug use presents with a 2-week history of fevers, chills, night sweats, and profound fatigue. He notes painful nodules on his fingertips and small, painless red spots on the palms of his hands. On auscultation, a new, harsh systolic murmur is heard best at the left lower sternal border.

presentationClues.description: History of IV drug use or prosthetic heart valve
Fever and new-onset heart murmur
Osler nodes (painful nodules on digits)
Janeway lesions (painless macules on palms/soles)
Splinter hemorrhages under the nails

vignette: A 30-year-old man with a known seizure disorder is brought to the ED by paramedics. He was found actively seizing with generalized tonic-clonic movements. The seizure activity has been continuous for the past 10 minutes without any return to baseline consciousness.

presentationClues.description: Continuous seizure activity for > 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them
Known history of epilepsy
Medication non-compliance
Ongoing tonic-clonic movements with unresponsiveness

vignette: A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol abuse is admitted to the hospital for pancreatitis. On day 3 of admission, he becomes agitated, confused, and is seen talking to someone who is not there. His heart rate is 130 bpm, blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg, and he has a coarse tremor of his outstretched hands.

presentationClues.description: History of heavy, chronic alcohol use
Onset of symptoms 48-96 hours after last drink
Autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, fever)
Altered mental status with agitation and hallucinations (visual)
Coarse tremor

vignette: A 48-year-old homeless man with a history of malnutrition and alcoholism is brought to the ED for evaluation of confusion. He is disoriented to time and place, has a wide-based, unsteady gait, and on physical exam displays bilateral horizontal nystagmus and paralysis of lateral gaze. He appears drowsy and apathetic.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, gait ataxia
Nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, or conjugate gaze palsy
Wide-based, ataxic gait
History of chronic alcoholism or malnutrition (thiamine deficiency)
Global confusion and apathy

vignette: A 62-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension suddenly collapses at home. His wife reports he complained of a severe headache and then became unresponsive. In the ED, his blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg, he is comatose, and demonstrates right-sided hemiplegia.

presentationClues.description: History of severe, uncontrolled hypertension
Abrupt onset of focal neurologic deficit that worsens over minutes
Symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, decreased consciousness)
Deeply comatose state early in presentation
Hyperdense (white) lesion within the brain parenchyma on non-contrast CT

vignette: A 40-year-old woman is brought in by her husband due to a 2-day history of fever, headache, and bizarre behavior. She has been unusually irritable, experienced olfactory hallucinations (smelling burning rubber), and had one focal seizure this morning. She is now confused and lethargic.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of fever, headache, and altered mental status
Bizarre behavior, personality changes, or psychosis
Focal seizures
Temporal lobe involvement (aphasia, hallucinations)
Hemorrhagic CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis

vignette: A 25-year-old woman presents with a recurrent, severe headache that she has experienced several times over the past year. She describes a preceding 20-minute episode of seeing flashing, zig-zag lines in her right visual field, followed by a unilateral, throbbing left-sided headache. During the headache, she feels nauseous and is extremely sensitive to light and sound.

presentationClues.description: Preceding transient neurologic symptoms (visual aura)
Scintillating scotoma (flashing lights)
Unilateral, pulsating/throbbing quality of headache
Photophobia and phonophobia
Associated nausea and/or vomiting

vignette: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of severe, excruciating headaches. He reports the pain is always behind his right eye, describing it as a 'hot poker', and lasts for about 45 minutes, occurring 1-2 times per day, often waking him from sleep. During an attack, his right eye tears up, his nose runs, and he feels intensely restless.

presentationClues.description: Severe, unilateral, periorbital/temporal pain
Attacks occur in cyclical clusters
Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, ptosis)
Restlessness or agitation during attacks
Male predominance

vignette: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a prosthetic right knee presents with an acute onset of severe right knee pain, swelling, and inability to bear weight. The pain began yesterday and has rapidly worsened. She has a fever of 101.5°F and on exam, the knee is erythematous, warm to the touch, and exquisitely tender with any attempted range of motion.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of monoarticular joint pain
Marked pain with passive range of motion
Signs of inflammation: erythema, warmth, swelling, effusion
Risk factors: diabetes, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression
Synovial fluid analysis: WBC > 50,000 with >75% neutrophils

vignette: A 42-year-old woman who sustained a minor crush injury to her left hand 6 weeks ago presents with persistent, severe burning pain in the entire hand. She describes the pain as being 'out of all proportion' to the initial injury. She notes her hand is now often swollen, discolored (blotchy red and purple), and feels colder than the other hand.

presentationClues.description: History of preceding trauma or surgery to the affected limb
Pain out of proportion to the inciting event
Sensory abnormalities: allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli) or hyperalgesia
Autonomic changes: swelling, temperature asymmetry, skin color changes
Motor/trophic changes: decreased range of motion, hair/nail growth changes

vignette: A 52-year-old woman presents to the ED with a sudden-onset severe headache that began 2 hours ago while exercising. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She has a history of polycystic kidney disease and hypertension.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache - sudden, severe onset
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity on examination
Photophobia present
Onset during physical exertion (Valsalva)
History of polycystic kidney disease (risk for berry aneurysm)

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought to the ED after being struck in the side of the head with a baseball. He initially lost consciousness for a minute, then seemed fine and was talking for about an hour. Now, he is increasingly drowsy, confused, and has vomited twice.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Direct trauma to the temporal region (middle meningeal artery)
Ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil (CN III compression)
Contralateral hemiparesis
Lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma on non-contrast CT

vignette: An 82-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation on warfarin is brought in by his family for evaluation of progressive confusion and gait instability over the past month. The family reports he had a minor fall about 6 weeks ago but didn't seek care. He complains of a mild, persistent headache.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient with history of minor head trauma
Anticoagulant use (warfarin)
Insidious onset of cognitive decline and gait changes
Crescent-shaped (concave) hematoma on non-contrast CT
Cerebral atrophy (risk factor - stretches bridging veins)

vignette: A 19-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. He is confused and has developed a petechial rash on his trunk and lower extremities. His roommate states he has been feeling unwell for the past day.

presentationClues.description: Nuchal rigidity
Positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
Living in close quarters (dormitory)
Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Petechial or purpuric rash (concerning for N. meningitidis)

vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus suddenly develops difficulty speaking and weakness on the right side of his body. His wife notes that his face began to droop on the right side while eating breakfast one hour ago. In the ED, he is alert but frustrated, unable to produce fluent speech.

presentationClues.description: Sudden, acute onset of focal neurological deficits
Contralateral hemiparesis (face and arm weakness > leg weakness)
Expressive aphasia (Broca's area - dominant hemisphere)
Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia
Vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes)

vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of progressive weakness and tingling that started in her feet and has now moved up to her thighs and hands. She reports having a diarrheal illness about two weeks ago. On examination, she has symmetric, flaccid paralysis of the lower extremities and absent deep tendon reflexes.

presentationClues.description: Ascending paralysis
Recent gastrointestinal or respiratory infection (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni)
Areflexia or hyporeflexia
Relatively symmetric weakness
Albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (high protein, normal WBC)

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with complaints of double vision and drooping eyelids that are worse in the evening. She also notes difficulty chewing her food and her voice becomes nasal and weak after talking for a while. She reports that these symptoms improve significantly after she takes a nap.

presentationClues.description: Fluctuating weakness that worsens with repetitive use
Symptoms improve with rest
Ptosis and/or diplopia
Bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia)
Diurnal variation (worse at the end of the day)

vignette: A 31-year-old female presents with a 3-day history of blurry vision and pain with movement in her right eye. She also reports a 'pins-and-needles' sensation in her left leg that occurred a year ago but resolved on its own. On exam, she has a right afferent pupillary defect and decreased color vision in that eye.

presentationClues.description: Optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss)
Neurological symptoms disseminated in time and space
