Positive Lhermitte's sign (electric shock down spine on neck flexion)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
Oligoclonal bands in CSF

vignette: A 67-year-old man is brought to clinic by his wife due to concerns about his slow movements and a tremor in his right hand. She notes his handwriting has become very small and he has a 'masked' facial expression. The patient reports feeling stiff and has difficulty initiating movements, such as getting out of a chair.

presentationClues.description: Pill-rolling tremor at rest
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement)
Cogwheel rigidity
Shuffling, festinating gait with postural instability
Micrographia (small handwriting)

vignette: A 45-year-old man is brought to the ED for acute onset of confusion, fever, and headache over the past 48 hours. His family reports bizarre behavior, including olfactory hallucinations (smelling burnt rubber) and one episode of a focal seizure. On exam, he is febrile, disoriented, and has difficulty naming common objects.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset of fever, headache, and altered mental status
Bizarre behavior or personality changes
Focal seizures
Temporal lobe involvement on MRI or EEG
Olfactory or gustatory hallucinations

vignette: A 30-year-old man with a known seizure disorder is brought to the ED by ambulance. He was found actively seizing with generalized tonic-clonic movements. The seizure activity has been continuous for the past 10 minutes without any return to consciousness, according to paramedics.

presentationClues.description: Continuous seizure activity for > 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them
Known history of epilepsy or recent medication non-compliance
Neurological emergency
Ongoing convulsive activity or non-convulsive state with profound coma

vignette: A 72-year-old woman presents with a new-onset headache, primarily over her left temple, for the past 2 weeks. She describes the pain as a constant, dull ache. She also reports pain in her jaw when she chews and some recent episodes of transient, curtain-like vision loss in her left eye.

presentationClues.description: Age > 50 years
Jaw claudication
New-onset headache
Tender, palpable temporal artery
Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss)
Markedly elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)

vignette: A 65-year-old woman complains of recurrent, sudden episodes of severe, stabbing pain on the right side of her face. The pain lasts only a few seconds but is excruciating, and it can be triggered by brushing her teeth, chewing, or even a light breeze on her cheek. The neurologic exam between episodes is completely normal.

presentationClues.description: Lancinating, electric shock-like pain
Pain located in V2/V3 dermatomes of the trigeminal nerve
Presence of specific trigger zones or actions
Paroxysmal attacks lasting seconds to minutes
Normal neurological examination between attacks

vignette: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of severe, unilateral headaches that wake him up from sleep every night. He describes the pain as a 10/10 sharp sensation behind his left eye. During the attacks, which last about 45 minutes, his left eye tears profusely and his nose becomes congested on that side.

presentationClues.description: Suicide headache - excruciating pain
Attacks occur in cyclical patterns or 'clusters'
Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis)
More common in males
Patient is often restless or agitated during attacks

vignette: A 58-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive weakness. He first noticed it as difficulty buttoning his shirt and frequent tripping, and now he has trouble speaking and swallowing. On exam, he has diffuse muscle wasting and fasciculations in his arms, as well as hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign bilaterally.

presentationClues.description: Upper and lower motor neuron signs
Lower motor neuron signs: fasciculations, atrophy, flaccid weakness
Upper motor neuron signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski
Progressive, asymmetric weakness
Sensation, bowel/bladder function, and cognition are spared

vignette: A 42-year-old woman presents to urgent care with an acute onset of right-sided facial paralysis that she first noticed this morning. She is unable to close her right eye, raise her right eyebrow, or smile on the right side. She also reports pain behind her right ear and says that sounds seem louder than usual.

presentationClues.description: Acute, unilateral facial paralysis
Inability to wrinkle the forehead on the affected side
Post-auricular pain preceding paralysis
Hyperacusis (increased sensitivity to sound)
Idiopathic CN VII palsy

vignette: A 40-year-old man is brought in by his wife who is concerned about his increasingly irritable mood, impulsive behavior, and abnormal, jerky movements over the past year. His wife mentions that his father had similar 'dance-like' movements and passed away in a nursing home. On exam, the patient displays brief, purposeless, and non-repetitive movements of his face, limbs, and trunk.

presentationClues.description: Chorea (involuntary, dance-like movements)
Autosomal dominant family history
Psychiatric disturbances (depression, psychosis, irritability)
Progressive cognitive decline
CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion

vignette: A 55-year-old homeless man with a long history of chronic alcohol abuse is brought to the ED for confusion. On examination, he is disoriented, has a wide-based, unsteady gait, and demonstrates horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze. When asked what he had for breakfast, he confidently describes a lavish meal that the paramedics state he did not have.

presentationClues.description: Classic Triad: encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia
History of chronic alcoholism / malnutrition (thiamine deficiency)
Nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy
Gait ataxia
Confabulation (invented memories)

vignette: A 48-year-old man with a history of chronic low back pain presents to the ED with a 12-hour history of worsening pain, bilateral leg weakness, and numbness in his groin area. He reports feeling like he needs to urinate but is unable to, and he had an episode of bowel incontinence this morning. He has a large midline disc herniation at L4-L5 on a prior MRI.

presentationClues.description: Saddle anesthesia
Bowel and/or bladder dysfunction (urinary retention is common)
Bilateral sciatica or leg weakness
Decreased anal sphincter tone on rectal exam
Surgical emergency

vignette: An 80-year-old woman is brought to her primary care provider by her daughter, who is concerned about her mother's memory. The daughter notes that her mother has been getting lost while driving in familiar neighborhoods, repeatedly asking the same questions, and has difficulty managing her finances. The patient seems unaware of her deficits and becomes irritable when questioned about them.

presentationClues.description: Insidious onset and progressive cognitive decline
Initial prominent impairment in recent memory
Visuospatial deficits (e.g., getting lost)
Impaired executive function (e.g., managing finances)
Beta-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles

vignette: An 85-year-old man with dementia is admitted to the hospital for a urinary tract infection. On day 2 of his stay, the nursing staff reports that he has become acutely agitated, is pulling at his IV lines, and seems to be hallucinating. His level of attention fluctuates throughout the day, alternating between drowsiness and hyper-arousal.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset and fluctuating course
Inattention (hallmark feature)
Caused by an underlying medical condition (e.g., infection, medication)
Disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness
Advanced age and pre-existing cognitive impairment are major risk factors

vignette: A 25-year-old female presents with a recurrent, unilateral, throbbing headache that lasts for 6-8 hours. She notes that for about 20 minutes before the headache starts, she sees shimmering, zigzag lines in her vision. During the headache, she is extremely sensitive to light and sound and feels nauseous.

presentationClues.description: Visual aura (e.g., scintillating scotoma)
Unilateral, pulsating/throbbing quality
Photophobia and phonophobia
Aura symptoms are fully reversible and develop gradually
Nausea and/or vomiting

vignette: A 62-year-old man with a long history of poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the ED after his wife found him unresponsive. Earlier in the day, he complained of a sudden, severe headache and then developed progressive left-sided weakness and slurred speech over 30 minutes. On exam, his blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg and he withdraws only to painful stimuli.

presentationClues.description: Focal neurological deficits that worsen progressively over minutes to hours
History of uncontrolled hypertension
Symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, decreased consciousness)
Severely elevated blood pressure
Non-contrast CT shows hyperdense (white) area within brain parenchyma

vignette: A 33-year-old woman is evaluated for 'spells' where she suddenly stops what she is doing and stares blankly for about 90 seconds. During these episodes, her husband notes that she makes repetitive lip-smacking and chewing motions and fumbles with her shirt buttons. After the spell, she is confused for several minutes and has no memory of the event.

presentationClues.description: Impairment of consciousness (staring blankly)
Automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing, picking)
Post-ictal confusion or amnesia of the event
May be preceded by an aura (e.g., epigastric rising sensation, deja vu)
Focal onset, most commonly from the temporal lobe

vignette: A 24-year-old male presents to the ED with a 2-day history of headache, low-grade fever, and photophobia. He reports feeling generally unwell since returning from a camping trip last week. On exam, he is alert and oriented, has mild nuchal rigidity, but Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are negative.

presentationClues.description: Subacute onset of fever, headache, and meningismus
Patient is typically non-toxic appearing and alert
CSF analysis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis
CSF glucose is normal, protein is normal or mildly elevated
Often caused by enteroviruses in late summer/early fall

vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a history of polycystic kidney disease presents to the ED with a sudden-onset severe headache that began 2 hours ago. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She was watching television when the headache struck with maximal intensity instantly.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity on examination
Photophobia and neck stiffness
History of polycystic kidney disease (risk factor for berry aneurysm)

vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation is brought to the ED after his wife noted he suddenly developed slurred speech and right-sided weakness. He appears confused and is unable to follow commands. Symptoms began approximately 90 minutes ago.

presentationClues.description: History of atrial fibrillation
Contralateral hemiparesis, with arm and face weakness greater than leg
Expressive aphasia (Broca's area involvement)
Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia
Sudden onset of focal neurological deficits

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought to the ER after being struck in the side of the head with a baseball bat. He lost consciousness for a minute, then woke up and seemed fine, talking to his teammates. About an hour later, he became progressively drowsy and then unresponsive.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Trauma to the temporal region of the skull
Ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil (CN III compression)
Contralateral hemiparesis
Associated with middle meningeal artery tear

vignette: A 20-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the ER by his roommate due to high fever, severe headache, and confusion over the last 12 hours. On arrival, he is lethargic and complains of a stiff neck. A petechial rash is noted on his trunk and lower extremities.

presentationClues.description: Nuchal rigidity (stiff neck)
Positive Kernig's sign
Positive Brudzinski's sign
Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Living in close quarters (dormitory)
Petechial rash (suggests N. meningitidis)

vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressive weakness and tingling in her feet that has now ascended to her knees and hands. She reports having a diarrheal illness about two weeks ago. On exam, she has symmetric, flaccid paralysis of her lower extremities and absent deep tendon reflexes.

presentationClues.description: Ascending paralysis
Recent history of Campylobacter jejuni or viral infection (URI)
Areflexia or hyporeflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes)
Symmetric weakness
Paresthesias often precede weakness

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of double vision and drooping of her eyelids that worsens as the day progresses. She notes that her symptoms are much better in the morning after a night's sleep. She also complains of difficulty chewing her food by the end of a meal.

presentationClues.description: Fatigable weakness
Symptoms worsen with repetitive use and improve with rest
Ptosis and/or diplopia, often as initial symptoms
Weakness worsens with sustained upward gaze (Cogan's lid twitch)
Normal sensation and reflexes

vignette: A 31-year-old female presents with a 4-day history of blurry, painful vision in her right eye and numbness in her left leg. She recalls an episode of 'pins and needles' in her arms about a year ago that resolved on its own. On exam, she has a right afferent pupillary defect and decreased sensation to light touch in her left lower extremity.

presentationClues.description: Neurological symptoms disseminated in time and space
Optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock-like sensation down the spine with neck flexion)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction of one eye)
Symptoms often exacerbated by heat (Uhthoff's phenomenon)

vignette: A 65-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a complaint of a tremor in his right hand that is most noticeable when he is watching television. His wife notes that his face seems less expressive and he has been walking more slowly, with a stooped posture. He also complains of a general feeling of stiffness.

presentationClues.description: Pill-rolling tremor
Asymmetric resting tremor
Cogwheel rigidity on passive range of motion
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement)
Shuffling gait with stooped posture

vignette: An 80-year-old man with a history of alcoholism and multiple falls is brought in by his daughter for evaluation of progressive confusion and gait instability over the past month. The patient seems apathetic and has a fluctuating level of consciousness. The daughter recalls he bumped his head a few weeks ago but didn't seek medical attention.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient or history of alcoholism (brain atrophy)
Minor head trauma weeks to months prior
Insidious onset of cognitive decline, headache, or gait changes
Bridging vein tear
Fluctuating level of consciousness

vignette: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents to the ER with the abrupt onset of a severe headache, vomiting, and right-sided weakness. He rapidly becomes lethargic. His initial blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg.

presentationClues.description: History of chronic, poorly controlled hypertension
Abrupt onset of focal deficit that worsens over minutes to hours
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, decreased consciousness)
Focal neurological deficits corresponding to the location of the bleed (e.g., basal ganglia, pons)
No lucid interval

vignette: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the hospital with a 3-day history of fever, headache, and progressive confusion. Her family reports she has had bizarre behavior and memory problems. On examination, she is disoriented to time and place and has difficulty naming common objects.

presentationClues.description: Prodrome of fever, headache, and malaise
Altered mental status (confusion, lethargy, personality changes)
Presence of focal neurologic deficits (e.g., aphasia, seizures) distinguishes it from meningitis
Most commonly caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)
Temporal lobe signs (aphasia, olfactory hallucinations, memory disturbance) are common with HSV

vignette: A 75-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her son, who is concerned about her memory. He states that for the past year, she has been misplacing items, forgetting appointments, and asking the same questions repeatedly. She recently got lost driving home from the grocery store, a route she has taken for 40 years.

presentationClues.description: Insidious onset and gradual progression of cognitive decline
Initial symptom is most often short-term memory loss (anterograde amnesia)
Difficulty with executive function (planning, problem-solving)
Visuospatial dysfunction (getting lost in familiar places)
Normal motor and sensory exam in early stages

vignette: A 30-year-old man with a known seizure disorder for which he is poorly compliant with medication is brought to the ER by ambulance. He was found actively convulsing, with tonic-clonic movements of all four extremities. Paramedics report the seizure has been ongoing for at least 10 minutes without a return to baseline consciousness.

presentationClues.description: Seizure lasting > 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness in between
History of epilepsy, often with medication non-compliance
Continuous tonic-clonic activity or postictal state without regaining consciousness
A neurological emergency

vignette: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent, severe headaches that she has experienced since her teens. She describes a 'zigzag' pattern of flashing lights in her right visual field that lasts for about 20 minutes, followed by a severe, throbbing, unilateral headache. The headache is associated with nausea and extreme sensitivity to light and sound.

presentationClues.description: Scintillating scotoma (visual aura)
Aura is a transient focal neurological symptom that precedes or accompanies the headache
Pulsating or throbbing quality
Photophobia and phonophobia
Headache is typically unilateral

vignette: A 40-year-old male complains of episodes of excruciating, unilateral retro-orbital pain that have been occurring nightly for the past two weeks. He describes the pain as a 'hot poker in the eye' and it lasts for about 45 minutes. During the attacks, his right eye becomes red and watery, and he feels compelled to pace the room.

presentationClues.description: Suicide headache
Attacks occur in cyclical patterns or 'clusters'
Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis)
Patient is agitated and restless during attacks
More common in men; often associated with smoking history

vignette: A 65-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of sudden, severe, electric shock-like facial pain on the right side of her face. The pain is triggered by chewing, brushing her teeth, or a light breeze on her face. Each episode lasts only a few seconds, but they occur in rapid succession, leaving her afraid to eat or talk.

presentationClues.description: Electric shock-like pain
Pain is located along the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (CN V)

The nursing staff reports that she has been agitated and confused, particularly at night, pulling at her IV lines. She is disoriented to time and place, and her attention fluctuates throughout the interview, at times being drowsy and then suddenly restless.

presentationClues.description: Acute onset and fluctuating course
Inattention (difficulty focusing or shifting attention)
Disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness
Common in elderly, hospitalized patients, especially post-op
Often precipitated by an underlying medical condition, infection, or medication

vignette: A 51-year-old man with a known history of chronic alcohol abuse and malnutrition is brought to the ED for evaluation of confusion. His girlfriend notes he has been very unsteady on his feet for the past week, stumbling frequently. On examination, he is disoriented, demonstrates a wide-based gait, and has bilateral horizontal nystagmus and lateral rectus palsy.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, gait ataxia
History of chronic alcohol abuse or malnutrition
Encephalopathy (confusion, disorientation, apathy)
Oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia)
Gait ataxia (wide-based, unsteady)
Caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency

vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presents to the ED with a sudden-onset severe headache that began 2 hours ago while exercising. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports associated nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. She has no prior history of migraines.

presentationClues.description: Thunderclap headache
Worst headache of my life
Nuchal rigidity and positive Kernig's sign
Onset during physical exertion (Valsalva)
History of polycystic kidney disease or smoking

vignette: A 19-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after being struck in the side of the head during a rugby match. He briefly lost consciousness but then felt fine and continued to talk for about 45 minutes. Now, he is increasingly somnolent, complains of a severe headache, and has vomited twice.

presentationClues.description: Lucid interval
Trauma to the temporal region (pterion)
Ipsilateral fixed and dilated pupil
Contralateral hemiparesis
Associated with middle meningeal artery tear

vignette: An 82-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation on warfarin is brought in by his family for a 3-week history of progressive confusion, gait instability, and intermittent headaches. He had a minor fall about a month ago where he hit his head but did not seek medical attention. He appears drowsy and is slow to respond to questions.

presentationClues.description: Elderly patient with history of minor head trauma
Anticoagulant use (warfarin)
Fluctuating level of consciousness
Tearing of bridging veins
Insidious onset of cognitive decline and focal deficits

vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of uncontrolled hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with an abrupt onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking that began 1 hour ago. His wife noted that his face seemed to droop on the right side. He appears frustrated as he is unable to form words correctly.

presentationClues.description: Contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss (face/arm > leg)
Expressive aphasia (Broca's area involvement)
Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia
Atrial fibrillation is a major risk factor
Abrupt onset of focal neurological deficits

vignette: A 19-year-old college student living in a dormitory is brought to the ED with a 24-hour history of high fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. On presentation, he is confused and has a diffuse petechial rash on his trunk and lower extremities. He complains of severe light sensitivity.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: fever, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status
Positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
Petechial or purpuric rash (suggests N. meningitidis)
Living in close quarters (dormitory, military barracks)
Photophobia and phonophobia

vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressive, symmetric weakness that started in her feet and is now affecting her thighs and hands. She reports tingling sensations in her hands and feet but no sensory loss. She had a diarrheal illness about two weeks ago but has otherwise been healthy.

presentationClues.description: Ascending symmetric paralysis/weakness
Recent history of Campylobacter jejuni infection or URI
Areflexia or diminished deep tendon reflexes
Relatively preserved sensation despite paresthesias
Albumino-cytologic dissociation in CSF (high protein, normal WBC)

vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with several months of fluctuating double vision and droopy eyelids that worsen as the day progresses. She also notes difficulty chewing her food and her speech becomes slurred after long conversations. She feels significantly better in the morning after a night of rest.

presentationClues.description: Fluctuating, fatigable muscle weakness
Ptosis and diplopia, often worsening with upward gaze
Symptoms improve with rest
Positive ice pack test (improvement of ptosis)
Associated with thymoma or thymic hyperplasia

vignette: A 31-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of blurry vision and pain with movement in her right eye. She also reports a tingling sensation in her left leg that started last week. She recalls an episode of profound fatigue and weakness in both legs a year ago that resolved on its own after a few weeks.

presentationClues.description: Neurologic symptoms disseminated in time and space
Optic neuritis (pain with eye movement, vision loss)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock sensation down the spine with neck flexion)
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
Relapsing-remitting pattern of symptoms

vignette: A 66-year-old retired accountant is brought to clinic by his wife due to concerns about his slowness of movement and a tremor in his right hand. He has noticed his handwriting has become very small and he has difficulty initiating walking. On exam, he has a blank, expressionless face and walks with a shuffling gait.

presentationClues.description: Pill-rolling resting tremor
Cogwheel rigidity
Bradykinesia (slowness of movement)
Masked facies and shuffling gait
Asymmetric onset of symptoms

vignette: A 58-year-old man with a long-standing history of poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the ED after his wife found him unresponsive. He had complained of a sudden, severe headache and then became progressively lethargic over 30 minutes. On exam, his blood pressure is 220/130 mmHg and he withdraws only to painful stimuli.

presentationClues.description: Poorly controlled, long-standing hypertension
Rapid progression of neurologic deficit (minutes to hours)
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (vomiting, headache, decreased consciousness)
Symptoms are not confined to a single vascular territory
Commonly occurs in basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum

vignette: A 45-year-old man is brought to the ED by his family due to a 2-day history of fever, headache, bizarre behavior, and confusion. He has been having olfactory hallucinations, smelling 'burning rubber,' and had a generalized seizure this morning. He has no significant past medical history.

presentationClues.description: Fever + altered mental status + focal neurologic findings
Bizarre behavior, personality changes, or hallucinations
New onset seizures
Temporal lobe involvement (associated with HSV-1)
Often preceded by a prodrome of flu-like symptoms

vignette: A 76-year-old woman is brought to her primary care provider by her daughter, who is concerned about her mother's memory. Over the past two years, she has been progressively more forgetful, frequently misplacing items and getting lost while driving in familiar neighborhoods. The patient seems unconcerned by her deficits and struggles with word-finding during the interview.

presentationClues.description: Insidious onset and gradual progression of memory loss
Initial impairment in recent memory (anterograde amnesia)
Difficulty with executive function (planning, organizing)
Visuospatial dysfunction (getting lost, apraxia)
Normal motor and sensory exam in early stages

vignette: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for recurrent episodes where he suddenly stops what he is doing and stares blankly for about 90 seconds. During these events, he makes repetitive chewing motions and fumbles with his shirt buttons. After the episode, he is confused for several minutes and has no memory of the event.

presentationClues.description: Aura (e.g., epigastric rising sensation, deja vu)
Automatisms (lip smacking, chewing, picking at clothes)
Impaired awareness or consciousness during the event
Postictal confusion or drowsiness
Episode duration typically 30 seconds to 2 minutes

vignette: A 42-year-old man with a known seizure disorder for which he is non-compliant with his medication is brought in by EMS. He was found actively convulsing, with tonic-clonic movements of all four limbs. The seizure has been continuous for the past 10 minutes without any return to baseline consciousness.

presentationClues.description: Seizure lasting > 5 minutes
Two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them
Abrupt withdrawal of antiepileptic drugs
Underlying CNS infection, trauma, or metabolic disturbance
Continuous or rapidly recurring convulsive activity

vignette: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent, severe headaches that she describes as a unilateral, throbbing pain behind her left eye. Before the headache begins, she sees flashing lights and zig-zag lines in her vision for about 20 minutes. The headaches are associated with significant nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, lasting 4-6 hours.

presentationClues.description: Scintillating scotoma or visual aura
Unilateral, pulsatile/throbbing quality
Associated nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia
Aura symptoms are fully reversible and develop gradually
Positive family history of similar headaches

vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of excruciating, sharp pain around his right eye, which he describes as a 'hot poker.' The attacks occur 2-3 times per day, often waking him from sleep, and last about 45 minutes each. During the attacks, his right eye becomes red and watery, and his right nostril is congested.

presentationClues.description: Suicide headache
Severe, unilateral, periorbital or temporal pain
Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhea)
Attacks occur in cyclical 'clusters'
Restlessness or agitation during attacks

vignette: A 62-year-old woman complains of recurrent, sudden episodes of severe, electric shock-like pain on the right side of her face. The pain lasts only a few seconds but is excruciatingly intense. The episodes are triggered by light touch, such as brushing her teeth, chewing, or a cool breeze on her face.

presentationClues.description: Lancinating, electric shock-like pain
Pain is in the distribution of cranial nerve V (V2/V3 > V1)
Presence of specific trigger zones or actions
Pain is paroxysmal, lasting seconds to minutes
Neurological exam is typically normal between attacks

vignette: A 35-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with a sudden onset of left-sided facial paralysis that she first noticed this morning. She is unable to close her left eye, raise her left eyebrow, or smile on the left side. She also reports ear pain on the left side and says food tastes different.

presentationClues.description: Unilateral paralysis of the entire face (forehead included)
Acute onset over hours to 1-2 days
Inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos)
Hyperacusis or altered taste
Idiopathic peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy

vignette: A 55-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive weakness and twitching in his right arm, making it difficult to write or use a key. He has also developed slurred speech and has had several choking spells when drinking liquids. On examination, he has visible fasciculations in his arms and tongue, with marked muscle atrophy in his right hand.

presentationClues.description: Combined upper and lower motor neuron signs
LMN signs: muscle atrophy, fasciculations, weakness
UMN signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign
Bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia)
Sensation, bowel/bladder function, and cognition are typically spared

vignette: A 42-year-old man is brought in by his wife for evaluation of increasingly erratic behavior, irritability, and jerky, uncontrolled movements of his limbs and face. His wife notes that his father had similar symptoms and died in a nursing home. On exam, the patient displays writhing, dance-like movements of his extremities and has difficulty maintaining a steady posture.

presentationClues.description: Chorea (involuntary, dance-like movements)
Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern (positive family history)
Triad of motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms
CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion
Athetosis (slow, writhing movements) and dystonia

vignette: A 48-year-old man with a history of chronic, heavy alcohol use is brought to the ED for confusion and unsteady gait. He is disoriented to time and place and seems to be making up stories to fill in memory gaps. On exam, he has horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze and is unable to walk without assistance due to a wide-based, staggering gait.

presentationClues.description: Classic triad: encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, gait ataxia
History of chronic alcoholism or malnutrition
Nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, or conjugate gaze palsy
Ataxic, wide-based gait
Caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency

vignette: A 72-year-old man with a history of atherosclerosis presents with the sudden onset of vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and difficulty walking. He also reports double vision and has slurred speech. On exam, he demonstrates dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, nystagmus, and a unilateral limb ataxia.

presentationClues.description: Crossed findings (e.g., ipsilateral facial deficits, contralateral body deficits)
Cerebellar signs: ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia
Cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria)
Vertigo, vomiting, and nystagmus (vestibular nuclei involvement)
Also known as posterior circulation stroke

vignette: A 78-year-old man presents with a one-year history of progressive gait difficulty, describing his feet as being 'stuck to the floor.' His wife also reports he has become more forgetful and has had several episodes of urinary incontinence over the past few months. On examination, he has a slow, broad-based, magnetic gait and demonstrates mild cognitive impairment.

presentationClues.description: Wet, wacky, and wobbly
Magnetic (shuffling, wide-based) gait
Urinary incontinence
Cognitive decline / dementia
Symptoms may improve after large-volume lumbar puncture

vignette: A 74-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of a new, localized headache over her left temple. She also complains of jaw pain when chewing and diffuse muscle aches in her shoulders and hips. This morning, she experienced a transient, curtain-like loss of vision in her left eye that lasted a few minutes.

presentationClues.description: New-onset headache in a patient > 50 years old
Jaw claudication
Tender, palpable temporal artery
Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss)
Strongly associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR)

vignette: A 45-year-old female administrative assistant presents with a 3-month history of numbness and tingling in her right thumb, index, and middle fingers. The symptoms are worse at night, often waking her from sleep, and she reports relief from 'shaking her hand out.' She notes increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks like buttoning her shirt.

presentationClues.description: Paresthesias in the median nerve distribution (first 3.5 digits)
Symptoms worse at night
Flick sign (shaking hands for relief)
Positive Tinel's sign (tapping over the carpal tunnel)
Positive Phalen's test (wrist flexion reproduces symptoms)
Thenar muscle atrophy in severe, long-standing cases
